SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES

NORTHWEST DISTRICT

Plaintiff,

 

   v.

   Case Number             Department

COURT’S [TENTATIVE] ORDER RE:

Motion for Summary Judgment,

or in the alternative, Summary Adjudication

 

                        

 

[THE FOLLOWING IS A TENTATIVE RULING IN THE ABOVE CASE]:

 

(1) Deny motion for summary judgment;

(2) Grant motion for summary adjudication as to the second, third, fourth, ninth, and tenth causes of action;

 (3) Deny motion for summary adjudication as to the first, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth causes of action.

 

I.                BACKGROUND

Plaintiff Ayus & Co, Inc. (“Plaintiff”) is a licensed contractor engaged in plumbing construction work. (Second Amended Complaint [“SAC”] ¶ 2.) Defendant R Brothers, Inc. (“Defendant”) acted as the prime contractor for three construction projects located at the John A. Sutter Middle School (the “Sutter Project”), the 68th Street Elementary School (the “68th Street Project”), and the David Wark Griffith Middle School (the “Griffith Project”). (SAC ¶¶ 10, 29, 42.) Plaintiff and Defendant entered into written subcontract agreements where Plaintiff was to perform plumbing work and provide related labor, material, equipment, and services, and Defendant was to pay for the services. (SAC ¶¶ 11, 30, 43.) There remains due and owing $50,645.52 for the Sutter Project, $74,665.31 for the 68th Street Project, and $23,721.68 for the Griffith Project.  (SAC ¶ 12, 31, 44.)

On November 10, 2022, Plaintiff filed a complaint against Defendant, Philadelphia Indemnity Insurance Company, and Does 1 through 100, alleging six causes of action.

On January 11, 2023, Ayus filed a first amended complaint against Defendant, Philadelphia Indemnity Insurance Company, and Does 1 through 100, alleging thirteen causes of action.

On February 3, 2023, Ayus filed a request to dismiss Defendant Philadelphia Indemnity Insurance Company and that Defendant was dismissed.

On September 5, 2023, Plaintiff filed a second amended complaint against Defendant, Philadelphia Indemnity Insurance Company, and Does 1 through 100, alleging causes of action for: (1) breach of written contract; (2) breach of oral agreement; (3) common count for work, labor, and services rendered – agreed price; (4) common count for work, labor and services rendered – reasonable value; (5) breach of written contract; (6) common count for work, labor, and services rendered – agreed price; (7) common count for work, labor and services rendered – reasonable value; (8) breach of written contract; (9) common count for work, labor, and services rendered – agreed price; and (10) common count for work, labor and services rendered – reasonable value.

On June 20, 2024, Cross-Complainants R Brothers, Inc. and Shahrooz Rostami (“Rostami”) filed a cross-complaint against Cross-Defendants Ayus & Co, Inc., Baba Osiname (“Osiname”) and Roes 1 to 50, alleging causes of action for: (1) breach of contract; (2) breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; (3) defamation per se; and (4) defamation per quod.

On January 5, 2026, Defendant filed a motion for summary judgment (the “Motion”). On May 14, 2026, Plaintiff filed an opposition. On May 22, 2026, Defendant filed a reply.

II.             PLAINTIFF’S OBJECTIONS

Plaintiff submits objections to Defendant’s evidence.

In response, Defendant argues Plaintiff violated California Rules of Court, rule 3.1354(b) by failing to reference the objections in Plaintiff’s separate statement and by not disputing certain undisputed material facts. (Defendant’s Response to Plaintiff’s Objections.) Defendant cites Hurley Construction Co. v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Co. (“Hurley”) (1992) 10 Cal.App.4th 533, 541 and Rio Linda Unified School Dist. v. Superior Court (“Rio Linda”) (1997) 52 Cal.App.4th 732, 741. (Defendant’s Response to Plaintiff’s Objections.)

In Hurley, supra, 10 Cal.App.4th at pp. 540-541, Hurley argued no competent evidence supported summary judgment because a declaration was inadmissible and lacked foundation. The Court of Appeal rejected that argument, stating: “Hurley admitted each of the facts listed in State Farm's separate statement of undisputed facts. In doing so, he waived any objection to the exhibits, discovery responses, and deposition testimony which formed the evidentiary basis of State Farm's separate statement.”

In Rio Linda, supra, 52 Cal.App.4th at p. 741, the Court of Appeal distinguished Hurley and stated:

The case is not remotely apposite factually. The express admission that a fact is true necessarily includes the admission the evidence on which it is based is admissible; presumably, an opponent would not admit to that which cannot be proven by the moving party. Here, by contrast, the School admitted nothing. It included an undisputed fact which was part of the record in the case and expressly explained separately . . . why the fact could not be used to support real party's complaint because it was inadmissible.

This case is distinguishable from Hurley, where Hurley admitted each of the facts. Here, Plaintiff has not admitted all of the facts. (See Plaintiff’s Separate Statement.) The court is not persuaded Plaintiff conceded each point by failing to dispute each undisputed material fact that was based upon the evidence.

California Rules of Court, rule 3.1354(b) states, in relevant part:

All written objections to evidence must be served and filed separately from the other papers in support of or in opposition to the motion. Objections to specific evidence must be referenced by the objection number in the right column of a separate statement in opposition or reply to a motion, but the objections must not be restated or reargued in the separate statement . . .

Plaintiff’s separate statement does not reference the objections. (See Plaintiff’s Separate Statement.) Thus, Plaintiff’s separate statement does not comply with California Rules of Court, rule 3.1354(b).

Defendant cites no authority permitting the court to overrule Plaintiff’s evidentiary objections because Plaintiff failed to refer to them in the separate statement. The court views this issue as a deficiency with Plaintiff’s separate statement, as opposed to a deficiency with Plaintiff’s evidentiary objections. Thus, the court will consider Plaintiff’s objections.

Defendant’s response cites authority permitting the court to take judicial notice of the referenced documents. (Defendant’s Response to Plaintiff’s Objections pp. 30-31.) Requests for judicial notice must be made in a separate document and must comply with California Rules of Court rule 3.1306(c). (Cal Rules of Court, rule 3.1113(l).) Defendant filed no request for judicial notice with the court. To the extent Defendant, in the response to Plaintiff’s objections, is requesting the court take judicial notice of the referenced documents, that request is denied.

The dates of completion of administrative work are more accurate in terms of providing an “all work” date of completion. Accordingly, the approximate dates of completion of “all work” for each Project are as follows: Griffith: 10/28/2018; 68th St.: 11/8/2019; Sutter: 4/16/2021.”

Lacks foundation and personal knowledge; speculative; hearsay; best and/or secondary evidence; improper conclusion/ultimate fact.

Overruled

Ex. A ¶ 39, “Ayus’s COPs were the notices of its claims seeking compensation for extra work ordered by RBI, and they were timely submitted as shown in the COP Submission Date table attached to at Ex. 20. In Section 16.3 of the General Conditions–which Ayus was obligated to follow due to its incorporation by Sections 2 and 3 of the Subcontractor Agreements–the conditions surrounding when a claim arise is set forth: “[T]he claim arises upon the issuance of a written final decision by the OAR denying in whole or in part CONTRACTOR’s Change Order Request.”

Lacks foundation and personal knowledge; hearsay; best and/or secondary evidence; improper conclusion/ultimate fact.

Sustained

Lacks foundation and personal knowledge; speculative; hearsay; best and/or secondary evidence; improper conclusion/ultimate fact.

Overruled

RBI served an amended response to RFP No. 18 in the first set of documents requests, responding that RBI was unable to produce any payment documents from the Griffith project because it no longer has possession of such documents and no longer has access to applicable bank records. RBI also responded that it had produced its payment records for the Sutter and 68th Street Projects. (Attached collectively hereto as Exhibit 1 is a true copy of Ayus’s two sets of document requests and RBI’s amended response to Ayus’s second set of RFPs served on March 26, 2026.) RBI was unable to provide any documents pinpointing the dates it received payment for Ayus’s change orders.”

Lacks foundation, personal knowledge, and authentication; hearsay; best evidence; improper conclusion/ultimate fact.

(Attached collectively hereto Exhibit 2 is a true copy of the three “Payment Advice” documents produced by RBI in discovery.) The only Payment Advice relevant to RBI’s statute of limitations defense is the Payment Advice for the 68th Street Project showing ACH initiated on 12/13/2019 in the amount of $589,113.63.”

(Attached hereto Exhibit 3 is a true copy of the Griffith payment application produced by RBI in discovery.)”

IV.           PLAINTIFF’S OBJECTIONS TO REPLY EVIDENCE

Plaintiff objects to Alon’s supplemental declaration and attached exhibit submitted with Defendant’s reply.

“The general rule of motion practice . . . is that new evidence is not permitted with reply papers. . . . ‘The inclusion of additional evidentiary matter with the reply should only be allowed in the exceptional case ...’ and if permitted, the other party should be given the opportunity to respond.” (Jay v. Mahaffey (2013) 218 Cal.App.4th 1522, 1537-1538.)

Plaintiff has not had an opportunity to respond to Alon’s supplemental declaration and the attached exhibit. The court will not consider the evidence Defendant submits with the reply.

V.              TIMELINESS

A motion for summary judgment “may be made at any time after 60 days have elapsed since the general appearance in the action or proceeding of each party against whom the motion is directed or at any earlier time after the general appearance that the court, with or without notice and upon good cause shown, may direct.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (a)(1).) “The motion shall be heard no later than 30 days before the date of trial, unless the court for good cause orders otherwise. The filing of the motion shall not extend the time within which a party must otherwise file a responsive pleading.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (a)(3).)¿ 

¿ 

Per Code of Civil Procedure section 437c, subdivisions (a)(2), (b)(2) and (4):

¿ 

Notice of the motion and supporting papers shall be served on all other parties to the action at least¿81¿days before the time appointed for hearing. If the notice is served by mail, the required¿81-day¿period of notice shall be increased by 5 days if the place of address is within the State of California, 10 days if the place of address is outside the State of California but within the United States, and 20 days if the place of address is outside the United States. If the notice is served by facsimile transmission, express mail, or another method of delivery providing for overnight delivery, the required¿81-day¿period of notice shall be increased by two court days . . . An opposition to the motion shall be served and filed not less than¿20¿days preceding the noticed or continued date of hearing, unless the court for good cause orders otherwise . . . A reply to the opposition shall be served and filed by the moving party not less than¿11¿days preceding the noticed or continued date of hearing, unless the court for good cause orders otherwise.¿ 

 

The Motion was originally set for hearing June 3, 2026. Defendant served Plaintiff with the Motion by electronic mail on January 5, 2026. (Motion pdf p. 29.) Defendant timely served the Motion more than 81 days, plus two court days, before June 3, 2026. The opposition and reply were also timely filed.

VI.           LEGAL STANDARD

“A party may move for summary judgment in¿an¿action or proceeding if it is contended that the action has no merit or that there is no defense to the action or proceeding.” (Code Civ. Proc., §¿437c, subd. (a)(1).)¿¿ 

“Code of Civil Procedure section¿437c, subdivision (c), requires the trial judge to grant summary judgment if all the evidence submitted, and ‘all inferences reasonably deducible from the evidence’ and uncontradicted by other inferences or evidence, show that there is no triable issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.” (Adler v. Manor Healthcare Corp. (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1119, original italics)

“A defendant moving for summary judgment has the initial burden of presenting evidence that a cause of action lacks merit because the plaintiff cannot establish an element of the cause of action or there is a complete defense.” (Gordon v. Continental Casualty Company (“Gordon”) (2024) 107 Cal.App.5th 89, 99.) “When the defendant moves for summary judgment, in those circumstances in which the plaintiff would have the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence, the defendant must present evidence that would preclude a reasonable trier of fact from finding that it was more likely than not that the material fact was true [citation], or the defendant must establish that an element of the claim cannot be established, by presenting evidence that the plaintiff ‘does not possess and cannot reasonably obtain, needed evidence.’” (Padilla v. Rodas (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 742, 747.)¿ 

“If the defendant satisfies this initial burden, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to present evidence demonstrating there is a triable issue of material fact.” (Gordon, supra, 107 Cal.App.5th at pp. 99-100.) To establish a triable issue of material fact, the party opposing the motion “must produce substantial responsive evidence[.]” (Sangster v. Paetkau (1998) 68 Cal.App.4th 151, 162-163.)¿Courts “liberally construe the evidence in support of the party opposing summary judgment and resolve doubts concerning the evidence in favor of that party.” (Gordon, supra, 107 Cal.App.5th at p. 99.)¿

VII.         DISCUSSION

Plaintiff alleges ten causes of action in the second amended complaint. The first through fourth causes of action relate to the Sutter Project. (SAC ¶¶ 9-27.) The fifth through seventh causes of action relate to the 68th Street Project. (SAC ¶¶ 28-40.) The eighth through tenth causes of action relate to the Griffith Project. (SAC ¶¶ 41-53.)

  1. Unclean Hands

Defendant argues Plaintiff’s claims are barred by unclean hands because Plaintiff was federally convicted of mail fraud and wire fraud in 2001, but Plaintiff’s president said on LAUSD’s Prime Contractor Prequalification Questionnaire he had not been convicted of a federal or state crime of fraud, theft, or act of dishonesty. (Motion pp. 12-14.)

In opposition, Plaintiff argues Defendant cites no analogous caselaw, the misstatements had no adverse impact on Defendant, the alleged conduct is not directly related to the harm, and Defendant’s own inequitable conduct creates triable issues and undermines its position. (Opposition pp. 11-13.)

“The unclean hands rule is settled in California that whenever a party who, as actor, seeks to set judicial machinery in motion and obtain some remedy, has violated conscience, good faith or other equitable principle in his prior conduct, then the doors of the court will be shut against him in limine; the court will refuse to interfere on his behalf to acknowledge his right, or to afford him any remedy.” (Pond v. Insurance Co. of North America (“Pond”) (1984) 151 Cal.App.3d 280, 289-290, original italics, brackets removed.) The party’s conduct must directly infect the cause of action before the court it cannot be unrelated improper past conduct. (Id. at p. 290.) “The actions of the party alleged to have soiled hands must relate ‘directly to the transaction concerning which the complaint is made; i.e., it must pertain to the very subject matter involved and affect the equitable relations between the litigants.” (Id.)

Defendant cites Pond, supra, 151 Cal.App.3d and Burton v. Sosinsky (“Burton”) (1988) 203 Cal.App.3d 562, 573-574 as examples where unclean hands was applied where a party obtained contracts through misrepresentation or concealment. (Reply p. 4.)

In Pond, supra, 151 Cal.App.3d at p. 187, the trial court granted Insurance Company of North America’s (“INA”) motion for summary judgment in part because there were no triable issues “as to whether Pond knowingly failed to disclose documents in the underlying litigation that he knew to be critical to INA's case, and thus was barred from relief in a malicious prosecution action against INA because of his unclean hands.” The Court of Appeal noted that Pond’s activities directly related to the malicious prosecution action because the indemnity suit was the entire basis of Pond’s claim. (Id. at p. 290.) INA submitted evidence showing Pond “knew of INA's intent that the higher pilot minimums applied at the time the policy was written, and that Pond was in fact not present during coverage discussions between Stafford of INA and Clarke of Mission, even though he had stated in the declaratory relief suit that he was present and understood that the lower pilot minimums were to apply, since he left before pilot minimums were discussed.” (Id.) Pond did not disclose a letter, to which Pond attached a copy of the pilot minimums from the old INA policy and a “draft response to INA's questionnaire which he had shown only to Mission's counsel and which contained directly contradictory statements as to his perception of the understanding as to coverage.” (Id.) The Court affirmed the trial court’s judgment, stating it was “correct in determining that Pond was barred from his malicious prosecution action by his unclean hands as a result of his violation of principles of good faith and good conscience.” (Id. at p. 292.)

In Burton, supra, 203 Cal.App.3d at p. 564-565, the trial court ruled Burton’s foreclosure on a mechanic’s lien was barred because Burton and Katotakis had conspired to defraud Sosinsky. The Court of Appeal noted:

There is substantial evidence that Sosinsky was overbilled by Katotakis and some of Sosinsky's payments were credited to another account. Pwyment in excess of Burton's invoices was returned by Burton to Katotakis. There is also substantial evidence to support the trial court's conclusion that Burton agreed to this arrangement and profited by the continued business relationship with Katotakis. Moreover, the record supports the conclusion that Burton knew at the time his actions were wrongful and even illegal.

(Id. at p. 571.)

Plaintiff does not dispute the following facts: Contractors become prequalified for LAUSD’s subcontractor list through Prequalification as a General Contractor with LAUSD. (Plaintiff’s Separate Statement No. 3.) To be eligible for selection, the contractor must be on the LAUSD’s Prequalified Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing subcontractor list. (Plaintiff’s Separate Statement No. 2.) Osiname was federally convicted of mail fraud and wire fraud in 2001. (Plaintiff’s Separate Statement No. 8.)

Defendant submits evidence Plaintiff, through Osiname, responded on the prequalification applications that neither the applicant, nor its owners, partners, officers, or managing employees had been convicted of a federal or state crime of fraud, theft, or other act of dishonesty. (Defendant Ex. 34 attached to Ex. B at pdf pp. 412, 422; Ex. 35 attached to Ex. B at pdf p. 429; Ex. 36 attached to Ex. B at pdf p. 434; Ex. 38 attached to Ex. B pdf p. 444; Ex. 39 attached to Ex. B at pdf p. 453; Ex. 40 attached to Ex. B at pdf p. 462.) Defendant also submits evidence it could not and would not have selected Plaintiff if Plaintiff was not on LAUSD’s preapproved list and would not have selected Plaintiff if it knew about Osiname’s federal mail and wire fraud convictions. (Defendant Ex. A ¶¶ 8-11.)

Plaintiff submits a declaration by Osiname indicating he believed the question at issue was a duplicate question, based on a slightly differently phrased question from a different part of the application, and the incorrect selection was an oversight. (Plaintiff Ex. A ¶ 12.) Plaintiff also submits evidence it later disclosed the conviction to the LAUSD. (Plaintiff Ex. 10 attached to Ex. A at pdf pp. 129-130.)

Although not cited by either party, the court finds Murillo v. Rite Stuff Foods, Inc. (“Murillo”) (1998) 65 Cal.App.4th 833, applicable here. In Murillo, supra, 65 Cal.App.4th at p. 845, the plaintiff used false resident alien and social security cards to obtain employment from the defendant. The Court of Appeal noted that “Plaintiff's misrepresentation went to the heart of the employment relationship and related directly to her wrongful discharge and contractual claims” and the unclean hands doctrine would bar those claims. (Id.) The Court further noted the plaintiff’s discrimination and tort claims arose from acts occurring during her employment. (Id. at p. 847.) The plaintiff had alleged sexual harassment. (Id.) The Court noted the “plaintiff's alleged injuries are not the consequences of her fraud but of Atilano's despicable conduct and her employer's tolerance of that conduct. There thus is no direct connection between her wrongdoing and the harm she suffered.” (Id. at pp. 851-852.)

Here, submitting false statements to obtain approval to be placed on a prequalified list is analogous to submitting false information to obtain employment. Although the court understands they are contractual in nature, Plaintiff’s causes of action here are related to whether Defendant properly paid Plaintiff. (SAC ¶¶ 14, 31, 44.) The court finds there is a lack of direct connection between Plaintiff’s wrongdoing and the harm suffered.

Finally, Defendant’s argument assumes Plaintiff would not have been placed on the prequalification list if Plaintiff had honestly answered the question about prior convictions. But no evidence has been provided to the court that a truthful answer would have disqualified Plaintiff from the prequalification list. The question at issue is under the “scorable” section of the questionnaire, as opposed to the mandatory requirements section. (See, e.g., Ex. 34 attached to Ex. B pdf pp. 412, 406.) The questionnaire required Plaintiff to obtain a minimum score, but Defendant submits no evidence showing answering “Yes” to the question at issue would have put Plaintiff below the minimum score, thereby disqualifying Plaintiff.

Defendant has not met its burden of showing all of Plaintiff’s causes of action are barred by unclean hands.

  1. Eighth to Tenth Causes of Action

 

    1. Section 9

Defendant argues the Griffith Project causes of action are barred because Plaintiff did not comply with Section 9’s 30-day requirement to provide written notice of claim relating to extra compensation for a disputed change order. (Motion pp. 17-18.)

In opposition, Plaintiff argues the LAUSD procedures superseded the subcontract, Defendant waived the written change order provisions through its conduct, and Section 9’s “Disputed Work” provision does not apply. (Opposition pp. 14-17.)

The elements of a breach of contract claim are: (1) existence of a contract; (2) plaintiff’s performance or excuse for nonperformance; (3) defendant’s breach; and (4) resulting damage. (Wall Street Network, Ltd. v. N. Y. Times Co. (2008) 164 Cal.App.4th 1171, 1178.) 

 

The elements of a common counts claim are: (1) a “statement of indebtedness in a certain sum, (2) the consideration, i.e., goods sold, work done, etc., and (3) nonpayment.” (Farmers Ins. Exchange v. Zerin (1997) 53 Cal.App.4th 445, 460.)

 

 Defendant submits Section 9 of the contract, which states:

 

Subcontractor hereby agrees to make any and all changes, furnish the materials and perform such work as Contractor may require, without nullifying this Agreement, at a reasonable addition to, or reduction from, the Contract Price stated herein and pro rata to the same. Subcontractor shall adhere to the plans and specifications unless a change is authorized in writing. Under no conditions shall Subcontractor make any changes, either as additions or deductions, without the written order of the Contractor and Contractor shall not pay any extra charges made by the Subcontractor that have not been agreed upon in writing by Contractor and, in no event, shall Contractor make payment or any such extra charges unless and until the Contractor itself receives payment. Subcontractor shall submit immediately to the Contractor written copies of it cost or credit proposal for changes in the work. Disputed work shall be performed as ordered in writing by the Contractor and the proper cost or credit breakdown therefore shall be submitted without delay by Subcontractor to Contractor. Subcontractor shall give written notice of claim relating to any disputed work for which extra compensation is asserted together with cost or credit breakdown within thirty (30) days after such work is performed (or lesser time if required under the Prime Contract) or Subcontractor shall be deemed to have voided and abandoned any claim therefore. If Subcontractor initiates a substitution, deviation or change in the Work which affects the expense or scope of the work or the expense of other trades, Subcontractor shall be liable for the expense therefore. No change, alteration or modification in or deviation from this Agreement or the plans or specifications, whether make in the manner herein provided or not, shall release or exonerate, in whole or in part, any surety on any bond given in connection with this Agreement and neither Owner nor Prime Contractor or Contractor shall be under any obligation to notify the surety or sureties of any such change.

 

(Defendant Ex. 1 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 22.)

 

Defendant also submits Plaintiff’s discovery responses, where Plaintiff stated it was “unable to identify the date it completed the work for each change order . . .” (Defendant Ex. 29 attached to Ex. B pdf p. 371.)

 

The court finds Defendant has met its burden here by presenting evidence Plaintiff was required to obtain written order from Defendant before making changes and Plaintiff was required to provide written notice within 30 days after the work was performed, but Plaintiff stated it was unable to identify the date work was completed. 

 

First, Plaintiff argues the LAUSD procedures superseded the contract. The court sustained Defendant’s objections to the evidence cited in Plaintiff’s separate statement. (Plaintiff’s Separate Statement Additional Material Facts Nos. 1-5.) The court does not consider this issue further.

 

Second, Plaintiff argues Defendant’s waived the procedures through its conduct. Plaintiff cites Frank T. Hickey, Inc. v. Los Angeles Jewish Community Council (1954) 128 Cal.App.2d 676, 682-683, which states “[t]he parties may, by their conduct, waive such a provision with the result that the subcontractor does extra work without a written order. If the circumstances indicate that the parties intended to waive the provision, the subcontractor will be protected.” (Opposition pp. 14-15.)

 

Plaintiff submits a declaration by Osiname, who states: “For the Griffith Project, RBI acknowledged that the change order work requested by LAUSD’s CDs was outside the original subcontract agreement and never challenged that they were valid change orders during the time the work was being performed by Ayus.” (Plaintiff Ex. A ¶ 9.)

 

The court finds this creates a triable issue of material fact regarding whether Defendant waived Section 9’s requirements by its conduct.

 

    1. Statute of Limitations

Defendant argues the eighth to tenth causes of action are barred by the statute of limitations because the last dates Plaintiff completed work on the Griffith Project was the week of April 16, 2018, through April 22, 2018. (Motion p. 19.) Defendant also notes that “[i]rrespective of Plaintiff’s work on the property, the project as a whole was completed when LAUSD issued a Notice of Contract Completion and Acceptance dated October 18, 2018.” (Motion p. 19 fn. 19.)

In opposition, Plaintiff argues there are genuine disputes regarding when the statute commenced. (Opposition p. 17.) First, Plaintiff argues Defendant has not met its burden of showing the causes of action are barred because Defendant’s payments to Plaintiff were not due until Defendant was paid by LAUSD. (Opposition p. 17.) Plaintiff notes Defendant’s “motion contains no evidence or analysis regarding when it received payment from LAUSD for each COP at issue for the projects.” (Opposition p. 18.) Plaintiff points to evidence showing Defendant produced during discovery the last payment application related to the Griffith project was dated April 24, 2020. (Opposition p. 18.) Plaintiff argues payments were due within 30 days, so “[a]ssuming that LAUSD timely made this payment, which [Defendant] has not proven, the earliest that [Plaintiff’s] claims could have accrued for the Griffith Project appears to be March 24, 2019.” (Opposition pp. 18-19.)

Actions based upon written contracts have a four-year statute of limitations. (Code Civ. Proc., § 337, subd. (a).)

Defendant submits payroll records indicating the last payroll period entered by Plaintiff was for the week of April 23, 2018, to April 29, 2018. (Defendant Ex. A ¶ 13; Ex. 2 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 39.) Defendant submits evidence it has no record of Plaintiff submitting a written notice of claim seeking extra compensation for Griffith Project change order before May 22, 2018 or before Plaintiff filed its amended complaint in January 2023. (Defendant Ex. A ¶ 14.) Finally, Defendant submits LAUSD’s Notice of Contract Completion and Acceptance, dated October 18, 2018. (Defendant Ex. A ¶ 15.) Defendant’s president, Shahrooz Rostami states the Notice of Contract Completion and Acceptance means “no other work is to be performed on the project.” (Defendant Ex. A ¶¶ 1, 15.)

Evidence showing when the last payroll period was entered does not show when payment was due. Likewise, although Rostami states the Notice of Contract Completion and Acceptance means “no other work is to be performed on the project”, Rostami does not state it means all payments were due at or before the date the notice was issued.

Defendant has not met its burden on this issue.

  1. Fifth to Seventh Causes of Action

 

    1. Written Contract

Defendant argues the breach of written contract cause of action fails because the parties did not enter into a written contract relating to the 68th Street Project. (Motion p. 20.)

In opposition, Plaintiff states Plaintiff proposed an amended contract with modifications to Defendant’s standard form. (Opposition p. 22.) Plaintiff argues “the Parties’ subsequent conduct demonstrates mutual assent to the written subcontract . . .” (Opposition p. 22.)

The fifth cause of action is for breach of written contract. (SAC p. 6.) Plaintiff alleges Plaintiff and Defendant “entered into or were to enter into a written subcontract agreement under which Plaintiff was to perform certain plumbing work, on the 68th Street Elementary School Project, and provide related labor, material, equipment and services for the same, and Defendants, and each of them, were to pay for such services.” (SAC ¶ 30.) Plaintiff alleges an unsigned copy of the contract is attached to the second amended complaint as Exhibit B. (SAC ¶ 30.) Plaintiff alleges that “Plaintiff and [Defendant] . . . understood and agreed to the terms as set forth in Exhibit B and agreed to be bound to that agreement in the event no final and signed written agreement exists.” (SAC ¶ 30.)

The parties agree they did not sign the 68th Street Project Subcontractor Agreement. (See Plaintiff’s Separate Statement No. 84.) However, the absence of signatures does not necessarily render contracts unenforceable. (Vita Planning & Landscape Architecture, Inc. v. HKS Architects, Inc. (“Vita”) (2015) 240 Cal.App.4th 763, 773.) “A ‘voluntary acceptance of the benefit of a transaction is equivalent to a consent to all the obligations arising from it, so far as the facts are known, or ought to be known, to the person accepting.’” (Id., original italics.) Thus, the absence of signatures here is not dispositive.

Defendant also submits Form Interrogatory No. 50.1(b), which states: “state each part of the agreement not in writing, the name, ADDRESS, and telephone number of each PERSON agreeing to that provision, and the date that part of the agreement was made . . .” (Defendant Ex. 26 attached to Ex. B pdf p. 344.) Plaintiff’s supplemental response stated “None to Responding Party's knowledge.” (Defendant Ex. 2 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 345.) Form Interrogatory No. 50.1(d) states “identify all DOCUMENTS that are part of any modification to the agreement, and for each state the name, ADDRESS, and telephone number of each PERSON who has the DOCUMENT . . .” (Defendant Ex. 26 attached to Ex. B pdf p. 344.) Plaintiff’s supplemental response stated “The Change Orders between and in possession of the parties for the three projects. This includes Change Order proposal 1-4 as to the Griffith project, 1-26 as to the 68th St. project, and 1-7 as to the Sutter project.” (Defendant Ex. 26 attached to Ex. B pdf p. 345.) Finally, Form Interrogatory No. 50.1(e) states “state each modification not in writing, the date, and the name, ADDRESS, and telephone number of each PERSON agreeing to the modification, and the date the modification was made . . .” (Defendant Ex. 26 attached to Ex. B pdf p. 344.) Plaintiff’s supplemental response stated “None to Responding Party's knowledge.” (Defendant Ex. 26 attached to Ex. B pdf p. 345.)

Plaintiff submits a declaration by Osiname, where Osiname states:

On or about April 3, 2018, I spoke with RBI’s President, Shahrooz Rostami. During our conversation, I informed Mr. Rostami that if my amended Subcontractor Agreement was not accepted by RBI, then RBI would have to find a new subcontractor, which would necessitate RBI’s filing of a Request for Substitution of Subcontractor with the LAUSD, and that process could be a protracted one. Mr. Rostami explained that he needed Ayus to begin work immediately and promised to sign to Ayus’s amended Subcontractor Contractor if Ayus would immediately begin work on an urgent basis. I accepted Mr. Rostami’s verbal acceptance of the Ayus-amended Subcontractor Agreement and promise to deliver a signed copy, and in exchange, immediately began work on the 68th Street Project. The parties both performed pursuant to the unsigned written agreement . . .

(Plaintiff Ex. A ¶ 35.)

The court finds Defendant met its burden of showing no signed contract relating to the 68th Street Project exists. However, the court further finds Plaintiff has met its burden by demonstrating there are triable issues of fact relating to whether Defendant accepted the terms of the contract.

    1. Statute of Limitations

Defendant argues that no written contract exists, so the fifth through seventh causes of action are governed by the two-year statute of limitations relating to implied contracts. (Motion pp. 20-21.)

The court is not persuaded the two-year statute of limitations applies here. In E.O.C. Ord, Inc. v. Kovakovich (1988) 200 Cal.App.3d 1194, 1196, the Court of Appeal considered whether the two-year statute of limitations based on oral contracts or four-year statute of limitations based on written contracts applied. The Court held the four-year statute of limitations applied, despite there being no written indication of the defendant’s acceptance of the terms of the written contract. (Id. at p. 1199.)

Defendant’s position these causes of action are barred by the two-year statute of limitations is incorrect. Defendant has not met its burden here.

  1. Eighth to Tenth and Fifth to Seventh Causes of Action

 

    1. Accord and Satisfaction

Defendant argues the eighth to tenth and fifth to seventh causes of action are barred by accord and satisfaction because Plaintiff accepted final payment for the Griffith Project and 68th Street Project. (Motion pp. 22-24.)

In opposition, Plaintiff argues there are genuine disputes relating to whether Defendant’s checks had a conspicuous notation and whether Plaintiff’s acceptance was inadvertent or without knowledge. (Opposition pp. 23-24.) Plaintiff also argues there is a lack of bona fide dispute here because Defendant concealed information from Plaintiff. (Opposition p. 24.)

“A defendant asserting the defense of accord and satisfaction must establish ‘(1) that there was a “bona fide dispute” between the parties, (2) that the debtor made it clear that acceptance of what he tendered was subject to the condition that it was to be in full satisfaction of the creditor's unliquidated claim, and (3) that the creditor clearly understood when accepting what was tendered that the debtor intended such remittance to constitute payment in full of the particular claim in issue.’” (Bill Finance Co. v. U-States Forwarding Services Corp. (2002) 95 Cal.App.4th 111, 126.)

As for the Griffith Project, Defendant submits evidence that it issued a check to Plaintiff dated October 29, 2018, which stated on the memo line, “Griffith MS – Final COPS’s[.]” (Defendant Ex. 13 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 150.) The check was cashed and debited on October 31, 2018. (Defendant Ex. 14 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 152; Ex. A ¶ 23.) Defendant submits evidence “COP’s” is shorthand for “Change Order Proposals” and that it “matches the term as provided on [Plaintiff’s] own proposal form.” (Defendant Ex. A ¶ 23.) Defendant’s records do not show Plaintiff struck “Final” payment notation before cashing the check and Plaintiff did not issue any invoices after cashing the check. (Defendant Ex. A ¶ 23.)

As for the 68th Street Project, Defendant submits evidence it issued a check to Plaintiff dated April 24, 2020, which stated on the memo line, “68th St ES – Change Orders Final[.]” (Defendant Ex. 16 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 156.) The check was cashed and debited on or about April 30, 2020. (Defendant Ex. 17 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 158.) Defendant’s records do not indicate Plaintiff struck the “Final” payment notation before cashing the check. (Defendant Ex. A ¶ 25.)

Plaintiff submits Osiname’s declaration, where Osiname states Plaintiff received two check that had words containing “final” in the memo lines but Osiname “did not understand from the memo lines that by cashing the checks [Osiname] was releasing [Osiname’s] pending claims.” (Plaintiff Ex. A ¶ 25.)

In reply, Defendant argues it is irrelevant pursuant to Commercial Code section 3301 that Plaintiff “claims it did not subjectively understand the checks to be a final payment, as evidenced by its subsequent conduct where [Plaintiff] supposedly ‘continued to seek payment on the unpaid change orders, including filing stop notices for amounts due.’” (Reply p. 10.)

Commercial Code section 3301 states:

“Person entitled to enforce” an instrument means (a) the holder of the instrument, (b) a nonholder in possession of the instrument who has the rights of a holder, or (c) a person not in possession of the instrument who is entitled to enforce the instrument pursuant to Section 3309 or subdivision (d) of Section 3418. A person may be a person entitled to enforce the instrument even though the person is not the owner of the instrument or is in wrongful possession of the instrument.

The court fails to see how Commercial Code section 3301 renders Plaintiff’s argument irrelevant.

Defendant also cites Civil Code section 1526 and Commercial Code section 3311 for the proposition that “[w]here a claim is disputed or unliquidated, the acceptance of a check that contains ‘the words “payment in full” or other words of similar meaning are notated on the check,’ constitutes an accord and satisfaction unless ‘the creditor protests against accepting the tender in full payment by striking out or otherwise deleting that notation.’” (Motion p. 22.)

Commercial Code section 3311, subdivision (b) requires a “conspicuous statement to the effect that the instrument was tendered as full satisfaction of the claim.”

The court reviewed the memo lines on the two checks at issue here and is not persuaded no triable issues of material fact remain here as to whether they contain conspicuous statements to the effect they were tendered as full satisfactions of the claims. The word “final” could refer to either the final change orders submitted, or as a final payment. These are not conspicuous statements showing the instruments were tendered as full satisfaction of the claims.  

  1. Ninth and Tenth and Third and Fourth Causes of Action

 

    1. Section 9

Defendant argues the Griffith Project and Sutton Project have written agreements, so common counts cannot be asserted with respect to the change orders for those projects. (Motion pp. 25-26.)

Plaintiff does not appear to dispute this point but instead appears to only argue Section 9 is not controlling because Defendant insisted on conduct that is more closely aligned with LAUSD’s general conditions and Plaintiff accepted this course of conduct. (See, e.g., Plaintiff’s Separate Statement No. 215.)

Defendant cites Hedging Concepts, Inc. v. First Alliance Mortgage Co. (“Hedging Concepts”) (1996) 41 Cal.App.4th 1410, 1419-1420 for the proposition “equitable entitlement to a quantum meruit payment is not implied where the parties have actual contract terms covering payment.” (Motion pp. 25-26.)

“[T]here is no equitable basis for an implied-in-law promise to pay reasonable value when the parties have an actual agreement covering compensation.” (Hedging Concepts, supra, 41 Cal.App.4th at p. 1419.) “Quantum meruit is an equitable theory which supplies, by implication and in furtherance of equity, implicitly missing contractual terms. Contractual terms regarding a subject are not implicitly missing when the parties have agreed on express terms regarding that subject. A quantum meruit analysis cannot supply ‘missing’ terms that are not missing. ‘The reason for the rule is simply that where the parties have freely, fairly and voluntarily bargained for certain benefits in exchange for undertaking certain obligations, it would be inequitable to imply a different liability....’” (Id.)

Plaintiff’s third cause of action for common count for work, labor, and services rendered – agreed price and fourth cause of action for common count for work, labor and services rendered – reasonable value relate to the Sutter Project. (SAC ¶¶ 23, 26.) Plaintiff’s ninth cause of action for common count for work, labor, and services – agreed price and tenth cause of action for common count for work, labor and services rendered – reasonable value relate to the Griffith Project. (SAC ¶¶ 49, 52.)

Plaintiff does not dispute that Plaintiff and Defendant entered into written contracts for the Sutter Project and Griffith Project. (Plaintiff’s Separate Statement Nos. 208, 210, 212, 214.) Plaintiff disputes that Section 9 of the parties’ agreements is controlling. (Plaintiff’s Separate Statement Nos. 209, 211, 213, 215.) The court sustained Defendant’s objections to the evidence Plaintiff relies on.

The court finds Defendant has met its burden of showing written agreements exist here. Plaintiff has not met its burden.

The motion for summary adjudication as to the third, fourth, ninth, and tenth causes of action is granted. 

  1. First Cause of Action for Breach of Written Contract

Defendant argues the Sutter Project breach of written contract cause of action fails because Plaintiff admitted it was paid in full, so Plaintiff cannot establish Defendant breached the Sutter Project agreement. (Motion p. 26.)

In opposition, Plaintiff argues it did not admit to receiving full payment and Defendant is not entitled to forfeiture of payment based on the subcontract’s paperwork terms. (Opposition pp. 24-25.)

In reply, Defendant argues that Plaintiff does not dispute Osiname signed the stop notice, stating the “Total value of the whole amount of labor and materials agreed to be furnished is: $58,000” and Plaintiff had been paid $58,000, and Section 9 of the parties’ agreement said Defendant “shall not pay any extra charges made by the [Plaintiff] that have not been agreed upon in writing by Contractor”, so “[t]he terms of Section 9 of the Agreement and [Plaintiff’s] Stop Notice admissions bar any further recovery, and no breach can be asserted, as [Plaintiff] admits it was paid in full pursuant to the terms of the Sutter agreement.” (Reply p. 11.)

The referenced Stop Notice states the “[t]otal value of the whole amount of labor and materials agreed to be furnished is: $58,000[.]” (Plaintiff Ex. 21 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 332.) It further states “[t]he value of the labor and materials furnished to date is: 7/16/2020 $108,792.59[.]” (Plaintiff Ex. 21 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 332.) It also states “Claimant has been paid the sum of: $58,000[.]” (Plaintiff Ex. 21 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 332.) Finally, it states “[a]nd there is due, owing and unpaid the sum of: $50,792.59.” (Plaintiff Ex. 21 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 332.)

Defendant argues the statement in the Stop Notice that the “[t]otal value of the whole amount of labor and materials agreed to be furnished is . . . $58,000” operates as an admission Defendant did not breach the contract. (Reply p. 11.) But the court is not persuaded the Stop Notice operates as an admission Defendant did not breach the contract because the Stop Notice also states there is due, owing and unpaid the sum of $50,792.59. (Plaintiff Ex. 21 attached to Ex. A pdf p. 332.)

Defendant also argues Plaintiff cannot show breach because Plaintiff did not comply with Section 9. (Motion p. 27.)

Plaintiff submits Osiname’s declaration, where Osiname states “For the Sutter Project, RBI acknowledged that the change order work requested by LAUSD’s CDs was outside the original subcontract agreement and never challenged that they were valid change orders during the time the work was being performed by Ayus.” (Plaintiff Ex. A ¶ 11.)

The same analysis of Section 9 applies here as above.

There are triable issues on this cause of action.

  1. Second Cause of Action for Breach of Oral Contract

Defendant argues there are no triable issues of material fact relating to the second cause of action for breach of oral contract because Plaintiff concedes no oral agreement exists with respect to the Sutter Project. (Motion p. 28.)

In opposition, Plaintiff does not directly address the second cause of action.

“The elements of a breach of oral contract claim are the same as those for a breach of written contract: a contract; its performance or excuse for nonperformance; breach; and damages.” (Stockton Mortgage, Inc. v. Tope (2014) 233 Cal.App.4th 437, 453.)

Plaintiff does not dispute no oral agreement exists with respect to the Sutter Project. (Plaintiff’s Separate Statement No. 239.) There are no triable facts as to this cause of action.

The motion for summary adjudication as to the second cause of action is granted.

VIII.      CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the motion for summary judgment is denied. The motion for summary adjudication as to the second, third, fourth, ninth, and tenth causes of action is granted. The motion for summary adjudication as to the first, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth causes of action is denied.

                                                                                                        Judge of the Superior Court

Case Number: 25VECV01511    Hearing Date: July 20, 2026    Dept: 107

 

 

 

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES

NORTHWEST DISTRICT

 

 

Kasra Majzoob,

Plaintiff.

 

   v.

 

Volkswagen Group of America, Inc., et al.

Defendants.

 

 

 

   Case Number             Department

          25VECV01511     107

 

 

COURT’S [TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: ¿ 

Compel Deposition and Compel Vehicle Inspection

 

[THE FOLLOWING IS A TENTATIVE RULING IN THE ABOVE CASE]:

 

Deny

 

I.                BACKGROUND

 

On April 17, 2024, Plaintiff Kasra Majzoob (“Plaintiff”) leased a 2024 Audi S3 (the “Vehicle”). (Complaint ¶ 9.) The Vehicle was defective.  (Complaint ¶ 11.)

 

On March 17, 2025, Plaintiff filed a complaint against Defendants Volkswagen Group of America, Inc., DCH Calabasas-A, LLC d/b/a Audi Calabasas, and Does 1 through 10, alleging causes of action for: (1) violation of Song-Beverly Act - breach of express warranty; (2) violation of Song-Beverly Act - breach of implied warranty; (3) violation of the Song-Beverly Act section 1793.2; and (4) negligent repair.

 

On June 8, 2026, Defendant Volkswagen Group of America, Inc. (“Defendant”) filed a motion to compel deposition of Plaintiff and production of documents (the “Motion to Compel Deposition”) and a motion to compel inspection of Plaintiff’s vehicle (the “Motion to Compel Vehicle Inspection”). On July 10, 2026, Plaintiff filed oppositions.

 

II.             PLAINTIFF’S OPPOSITIONS

 

Oppositions are due to be filed and served at least nine court days before the hearing. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1005, subd. (b).)  Plaintiff filed oppositions only six court days before the hearing. Plaintiff’s oppositions are untimely and the court does not consider them.

 

III.           MOTION TO COMPEL DEPOSITION

 

  1. Meet and Confer

 

A motion to compel a deposition must “be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration under section 2016.040, or, when the deponent fails to attend the deposition and produce the documents, electronically stored information, or things described in the deposition notice, by a declaration stating that the petitioner has contacted the deponent to inquire about the nonappearance.”  (Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.450, subd. (b)(2).)

Code of Civil Procedure section 2016.040, subdivision (a) requires the meet and confer declaration to “state facts showing a reasonable and good faith attempt, either in person, by telephone, or by videoconference, to informally resolve each issue presented by the motion.”

 

Defendant’s counsel submits a declaration stating they sent Plaintiff’s counsel a letter requesting Plaintiff’s availability for a deposition and asking Plaintiff to provide dates. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 3.) Defendant served a notice of deposition that included a meet and confer letter. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 4.) Plaintiff did not respond and Defendant took a certificate of non-appearance at the deposition. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 5.) Defendant’s counsel followed up by email regarding alternative deposition dates. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 7.)

 

Defendant’s counsel’s declaration does not show Defendant’s counsel specifically inquired about Plaintiff’s nonappearance. Further, Defendant’s counsel’s declaration suggests the meet and confer efforts took place only via email. Meeting and conferring under Code of Civil Procedure section 2016.040, subdivision (a) must be done in person, by telephone, or by video conference. Meeting and conferring by email is insufficient.

 

Defendant failed to satisfy the meet and confer requirement.

 

  1. Legal Standard

 

“Any party may obtain discovery within the scope delimited by Chapter 2 (commencing with¿Section 2017.010), and subject to the restrictions set forth in Chapter 5 (commencing with¿Section 2019.010), by taking in California the oral deposition of any person, including any party to the action. The person deposed may be a natural person, an organization such as a public or private corporation, a partnership, an association, or a governmental agency.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.010.)  

 

An oral deposition “shall be scheduled for a date at least 10 days after service of the deposition notice.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.270, subd. (a).)  “The service of a deposition notice under Section 2025.240 is effective to require any deponent who is a party to the action or an officer, director, managing agent, or employee of a party to attend and to testify, as well as to produce any document, electronically stored information, or tangible thing for inspection and copying.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.280, subd. (a).)  

 

“If, after service of a deposition notice, a party to the action or an officer, director, managing agent, or employee of a party, or a person designated by an organization that is a party under¿Section 2025.230, without having served a valid objection under¿Section 2025.410, fails to appear for examination, or to proceed with it, or to produce for inspection any document, electronically stored information,¿or tangible thing described in the deposition notice, the party giving the notice may move for an order compelling the deponent's attendance and testimony, and the production for inspection of any document, electronically stored information,¿or tangible thing described in the deposition notice.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.450, subd. (a).)¿¿ 

 

“Any party served with a deposition notice that does not comply with Article 2 (commencing with¿Section 2025.210) waives any error or irregularity unless that party promptly serves a written objection specifying that error or irregularity at least three calendar days prior to the date for which the deposition is scheduled, on the party seeking to take the deposition and any other attorney or party on whom the deposition notice was served.”(Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.410, subd. (a).) 

 

  1. Discussion

 

Defendant moves for an order requiring Plaintiff to appear for deposition within fifteen days. (Motion p. 7.) Defendant’s counsel submits a declaration, stating:

 

On March 28, 2025, Defendant served a representation letter on Plaintiff’s counsel advising that Defendant intended to take Plaintiff’s deposition and inspect the Subject Vehicle within the next 120 days. The letter requested Plaintiff’s availability for both the deposition and the vehicle inspection and asked Plaintiff to provide five potential dates.

 

On May 21, 2025, Defendant served a Notice of Deposition, scheduling the deposition for March 13, 2025. Defendant included a meet-and-confer letter advising Plaintiff’s counsel:

 

“If we do not receive alternative dates by February 14, 2025, we will assume you and your client are agreeable to the date noticed and move forward with the deposition. If Plaintiff fails to appear, we will take a certificate of nonappearance and file a motion to compel Plaintiff’s deposition.”

 

Defendant did not hear from Plaintiff nor receive any alternative availability. Accordingly, on July 31, 2025, Defendant proceeded with the deposition and took a certificate of non-appearance as indicated in its notice.

 

(Roberson Declaration ¶¶ 3-5.)

 

Defendant’s counsel’s declaration sets forth an implausible sequence of events. Defendant’s counsel purportedly served Plaintiff with a notice of deposition on May 21, 2025, which set the deposition for March 13, 2025. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 3.) Assuming that is true, Defendant’s counsel noticed the deposition more than two months after the deposition was set to take place. Further, the meet and confer letter purportedly attached to the notice of deposition requested Plaintiff’s counsel provide alternative dates by February 14, 2025. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 4.) It is impossible for Plaintiff’s counsel to have provided alternative dates by February 14, 2025, when the letter was purportedly served to Plaintiff’s counsel on May 21, 2025, almost three months after the deadline. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 4.) Further, Defendant’s counsel’s declaration states the deposition proceeded on July 31, 2025. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 5.) The deposition notice purportedly set the deposition for March 13, 2025, so it is unclear to the court why Defendant would have proceeded with a deposition on July 31, 2025. (Roberson Declaration ¶¶ 4-5.)

 

Defendant’s counsel also states that on September 9, 2025, Plaintiff provided alternative dates for the deposition. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 6.) Defendant selected October 28, 2025, but was unable to proceed on that date due to a family emergency. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 6.) Defendant’s counsel followed up regarding alternative deposition dates. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 7.) On January 27, 2026, Defendant served another notice of deposition that set the deposition for February 13, 2026. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 8.) Defendant’s counsel states that “[t]o date, Defendant has not received a proposed date for Plaintiff’s deposition. Defendant has attempted to avoid filing a motion in order to conserve judicial resources, but further informal meet-and-confer efforts have proven futile.” (Roberson Declaration ¶ 9.)

 

Defendant’s counsel’s declaration sets forth an implausible sequence of events regarding the first deposition notice. The second deposition date was cancelled due to Defendant’s counsel’s family emergency. As for the January 17, 2026, notice of deposition setting the deposition for February 13, 2026, Defendant’s counsel’s declaration does not state Plaintiff failed to appear. It also does not reference Plaintiff’s objections, which are referenced in an email attached to the declaration. (Roberson Declaration Ex. A pdf pp. 12.)

 

Defendant has not shown it served Plaintiff with a valid deposition notice or that Plaintiff failed to properly object or appear at the deposition. Defendant’s Motion to Compel Deposition is denied.

 

Alternatively, Defendant requests a 120-day continuance of the trial date to complete fact discovery. (Motion to Compel Deposition p. 7.)

 

California Rules of Court, rule 3.1332(c) provides that “[a] party's excused inability to obtain essential testimony, documents, or other material evidence despite diligent efforts” may constitute good cause to continue trial.

 

As noted above, Defendant’s counsel’s declaration sets forth an implausible sequence of events. The court is not persuaded Defendant has made diligent efforts to complete Plaintiff’s deposition notice, such that Defendant’s failure to complete the deposition is excused.

 

IV.           MOTION TO COMPEL VEHICLE INSPECTION

 

  1. Meet and Confer

 

Motions brought under Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.310 must be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration under Code of Civil Procedure section 2016.040. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.310, subd. (b)(2).)

 

Code of Civil Procedure section 2016.040, subdivision (a) requires the meet and confer declaration to “state facts showing a reasonable and good faith attempt, either in person, by telephone, or by videoconference, to informally resolve each issue presented by the motion.”

 

Defendant’s counsel’s declaration references only meet and confer efforts taking place via email. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 5.) Under Code of Civil Procedure section 2016.040, subdivision (a), meeting and conferring must take place in person, by telephone, or by videoconference. Meeting and conferring by email is insufficient.

 

Defendant failed to satisfy the meet and confer requirement.

 

  1. Legal Standard

“On receipt of a response to a demand for inspection, copying, testing, or sampling, the demanding party may move for an order compelling further response to the demand if the demanding party deems that any of the following apply: (1) A statement of compliance with the demand is incomplete. (2) A representation of inability to comply is inadequate, incomplete, or evasive. (3) An objection in the response is without merit or too general.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.310, subd. (a).) “The motion shall set forth specific facts showing good cause justifying the discovery sought by the demand.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.310, subd. (b)(1).)¿¿¿¿ 

“In a motion under subdivision (a) relating to the production of electronically stored information, the party or affected person objecting to or opposing the production, inspection, copying, testing, or sampling of electronically stored information on the basis that the information is from a source that is not reasonably accessible because of the undue burden or expense shall bear the burden of demonstrating that the information is from a source that is not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or expense.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.310, subd. (d).)¿¿¿ 

  1. Discussion

 

Defendant moves under Code of Civil Procedure sections 2031.310 and 2023.010 for an order requiring Plaintiff to produce the Vehicle for inspection. (Motion pp. 2, 5.)

 

Motions to compel further responses to demands for inspection of documents or tangible things must be accompanied by a separate statement. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1345(a)(3).) Defendant filed no separate statement with the court.

 

Plaintiff served Defendant with objections to Defendant’s demand for vehicle inspection. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 4; Ex. A pdf pp. 8-10.) Defendant references the objections in the Motion, but otherwise fails to substantively address them. (Motion p. 3.) Defendant has not shown Plaintiff’s objections are without merit or too general. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.310, subd. (a)(3).)

 

Finally, motions brought under Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.310 must be filed within 45-days after service of the response. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.310, subd. (c).) Electronic service extends the deadline by two court days. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1010.6, subd. (a)(3)(B).) Plaintiff served Defendant with objections by electronic mail on February 17, 2026. (Roberson Declaration ¶ 4; Ex. A pdf p. 11.) Forty-five days, plus two days for electronic service, after February 17, 2026, was April 7, 2026. Defendant filed the Motion to Compel Vehicle Inspection on June 8, 2026. Thus, the Motion to Compel Vehicle Inspection is untimely.

 

V.              CONCLUSION

 

For the foregoing reasons, the Motion to Compel Deposition and Motion to Compel Vehicle Inspection are denied.

COURT’S [TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: ¿ 

Motion to be Relieved as Counsel – Defendant Associated Construction, LLC’s Counsel, Simrandeep S. Tiwana

 

 

[THE FOLLOWING IS A TENTATIVE RULING IN THE ABOVE CASE]: Denied

 

Counsel filed a proof of service showing Counsel served Plaintiff Doka USA, LTD. and Defendant Associated Construction, LLC with the notice of motion and motion, declaration, and proposed order. The proof of service does not show Counsel served Defendant 6801 Canoga, LLC. The court understands that Counsel was Defendant 6801 Canoga, LLC’s counsel until the substitution of attorney was filed on June 9, 2026. But Counsel must show 6801 Canoga, LLC was served with the notice of motion and motion, declaration, and proposed order. Therefore, the motion is DENIED.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Dated:             July 20, 2026                                      Hon. Eric Harmon

                                                                                    Judge of the Superior Court

Case Number: 25VECV06407    Hearing Date: July 20, 2026    Dept: 107

 

 

 

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES

NORTHWEST DISTRICT

 

Bilaal Salaam,

 

Plaintiff.

 

   v.

 

Jada Pinkett Smith,

Defendant.

 

 

 

   Case Number             Department

  25VECV06407                  107

 

 

COURT’S [TENTATIVE] ORDER RE:       

Motion Judicial Determination of

Protective Order Disputes and Entry of Plaintiff's

Proposed Protective Order

 

[THE FOLLOWING IS A TENTATIVE RULING IN THE ABOVE CASE]: Deny

 

I.                BACKGROUND

On November 7, 2025, Plaintiff Bilaal Salaam aka Brother Bilaal (“Plaintiff”) filed a complaint against Defendant Jada Pinkett Smith (“Defendant”) alleging three causes of action for intentional infliction of emotional distress.

On February 5, 2025, Defendant filed a special motion to strike under CCP section 425.16 (Anti-SLAPP motion) (the “Anti-SLAPP Motion”).

On April 13, 2026, the court denied the Anti-SLAPP Motion, in part, and granted it, in part. (04/13/26 Minute Order p. 17.)

On June 12, 2026, Plaintiff filed a motion for judicial determination of protective order disputes and entry of Plaintiff’s proposed protective order (the “Motion”). On July 7, 2026, Defendant filed an opposition. On July 13, 2026, Plaintiff filed a reply.

II.             MEET AND CONFER 

 

Motions for a protective order must be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration. (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 2031.060, subd. (a), 2030.090, subd. (a), 2025.420, subd. (a).) “A meet and confer declaration in support of a motion shall state facts showing a reasonable and good faith attempt, either in person, by telephone, or by videoconference, to informally resolve each issue presented by the motion.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2016.040, subd. (a).

 

Plaintiff states they “transmitted meet and confer correspondence” and attaches copies of that correspondence as Exhibit B. (Salaam Declaration ¶ 2.) Defendant’s counsel responded by email and letter. (Salaam Declaration ¶ 3.)

 

Code of Civil Procedure section 2016.040, subdivision (a) requires meeting and conferring in person, by telephone, or by videoconference. Meeting and conferring by email and letter are insufficient. Thus, Plaintiff did not satisfy the meet and confer requirement.

III.           LEGAL STANDARD

Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.060, subdivision (a) states, in relevant part: “[w]hen an inspection, copying, testing, or sampling of documents, tangible things, places, or electronically stored information has been demanded, the party to whom the demand has been directed, and any other party or affected person, may promptly move for a protective order.” Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.060, subdivision (b) states, in relevant part: “[t]he court, for good cause shown, may make any order that justice requires to protect any party or other person from unwarranted annoyance, embarrassment, or oppression, or undue burden and expense.”

Code of Civil Procedure section 2030.090, subdivision (a) states, in relevant part: “[w]hen interrogatories have been propounded, the responding party, and any other party or affected natural person or organization may promptly move for a protective order.” Code of Civil Procedure section 2030.090, subdivision (b) states, in relevant part: “[t]he court, for good cause shown, may make any order that justice requires to protect any party or other natural person or organization from unwarranted annoyance, embarrassment, or oppression, or undue burden and expense.”

Code of Civil Procedure section 2025.420, subdivision (a) states, in relevant part: “[b]efore, during, or after a deposition, any party, any deponent, or any other affected natural person or organization may promptly move for a protective order.” Code of Civil Procedure section 2025.420, subdivision (b) states, in relevant part: “[t]he court, for good cause shown, may make any order that justice requires to protect any party, deponent, or other natural person or organization from unwarranted annoyance, embarrassment, or oppression, or undue burden and expense.”

“[T]he burden is on the party seeking the protective order to show good cause for whatever order is sought.” (Fairmont Ins. Co. v. Superior Court (“Fairmont”) (2000) 22 Cal.4th 245, 255.)

 

IV.           DISCUSSION

 

Plaintiff moves for an order entering Plaintiff’s proposed protective order. (Motion p. 2.) Alternatively, Plaintiff moves for a “judicial determination of the specific disputed provisions of Defendant’s proposed order that the parties have been unable to resolve through good-faith meet and confer efforts” and “[a] express finding that the Proposed Protective Order does not apply to testimony, exhibits, or court records already disclosed in prior public judicial proceedings, including Case No. 25VERO01692 . . .” (Motion p. 2.)

 

In opposition, Defendant agrees a protective order should be entered. (Opposition p. 2.) Defendant argues the Los Angeles Superior Court’s standard protective order is sufficient here. (Opposition p. 3.) Defendant further argues Plaintiff’s proposed modifications are not necessary. (Opposition pp. 3-5.)

 

In reply, Plaintiff argues Defendant’s opposition is speculative because Defendant cites no evidence showing Plaintiff intends to provide deposition testimony or video to the media or showing Plaintiff improperly disclosed confidential discovery. (Reply p. 4.) Plaintiff further argues Defendant identifies no prejudice that may result from Plaintiff’s proposed language. (Reply p. 7.)

 

Plaintiff argues good cause exists to enter the proposed protected order because Defendant’s proposed order’s mechanism to challenge a confidential designation is deficient. (Motion p. 6.) Plaintiff also argues Defendant’s testimony in a prior case cannot be retroactively restricted by a protective order. (Motion p. 7.) Plaintiff identifies three disputed provisions in Defendant’s proposed protective order. (Motion p. 8.) First, Plaintiff argues Defendant’s proposed protective order may designate Plaintiff’s own information and information Plaintiff possessed prior to this litigation as confidential. (Motion p. 8.) Second, Plaintiff argues Paragraph 13 of Defendant’s proposed protective order does not adequately address a party’s right to report information to law enforcement, regulatory agencies, or prosecutorial authorities. (Motion p. 8.) Finally, Plaintiff argues Paragraph 8 in Defendant’s proposed protective order “restricts use of Confidential Materials to purposes related to this litigation ‘and not for any business or other purpose whatsoever.’” (Motion p. 8.) Plaintiff argues this “restricts Plaintiff from using or discussing information that was produced in discovery but that he independently possessed outside of the discovery process.” (Motion pp. 8-9.) Plaintiff argues Plaintiff’s proposed protective order resolves these issues. (Motion p. 9.)

 

It is unclear whether Plaintiff attached Plaintiff’s proposed protective order to the Motion. Plaintiff’s declaration states it is attached as Exhibit A. (Salaam Declaration ¶ 10.) The page identified as Exhibit A does not appear to contain the full protective order. (Salaam Declaration Ex. A pdf p. 14.) Plaintiff’s proposed protective order may be attached as pdf pages 31 to 33. 

 

Plaintiff also failed to attach Defendant’s proposed protective order to the Motion. Likewise, Defendant references an “Exhibit A” attached to the opposition. (Opposition p. 2.) But no Exhibit A is attached to Defendant’s opposition.

 

The parties agree a protective order is necessary in this matter. (Motion p. 4; Opposition p. 2.) Plaintiff’s concerns surround information Plaintiff possessed prior to the litigation, Plaintiff’s right to report information to law enforcement, regulatory agencies, and prosecutorial authorities, and restrictions relating to how the information may be used. (Motion p. 8.) Based on Defendant’s opposition, it appears Defendant’s proposed protective order is the Los Angeles County Superior Court Model Protective Order. (Opposition p. 3.) Plaintiff identifies no specific language in the Los Angeles County Superior Court Model Protective Order applying to information Plaintiff possessed prior to the litigation or restricting Plaintiff’s right to report information to law enforcement, regulatory agencies, and prosecutorial authorities. The court is not persuaded Plaintiff has shown good cause for Plaintiff’s proposed protective order.

 

Plaintiff also requests a “judicial determination of the specific disputed provisions of Defendant’s proposed order that the parties have been unable to resolve . . .” and “[a]n express finding that the Proposed Protective Order does not apply to testimony, exhibits, or court records already disclosed in prior public judicial proceedings, including Case No. 25VERO01692 . . .” (Motion p. 2.)

 

Plaintiff argues the process to determine whether materials are confidential is insufficient because it is a “reactive remedy.” (Motion p. 6.) Plaintiff appears to request the court order testimony from Case No. 25VERO01692 be deemed non-confidential. (Motion p. 7.) Plaintiff argues that the testimony is part of the official public court record. (Motion p. 7.) In opposition, Defendant argues that “Plaintiff’s concerns regarding testimony from the prior civil harassment proceeding are . . . misplaced because the proposed order simply does not reach those materials.”

 

Defendant agrees the testimony from Case No. 25VERO01692 is not covered by Defendant’s proposed protective order. Thus, there is no dispute here for the court to resolve.

 

To the extent Plaintiff is requesting the court issue an order determining other testimony, exhibits, or court records are also not confidential, that request is denied. Defendant does not appear to be arguing such testimony, exhibits, or court records are confidential, so this request is premature.

 

V.              CONCLUSION

 

For the foregoing reasons, the Motion is denied.

Case Number: 26VECV02754     Hearing Date: July 20, 2026    Dept: 107

 

 

 

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES

NORTHWEST DISTRICT

 

Pedram Naeimiyan,

 

Plaintiff.

 

   v.
